text.text: Political violence is a growing global concern.
Across four preregistered studies (N=3,439), we examined perceptions of support for political violence within the United States (Studies 1-3) and India (Study 4).
In Study 1, Democrats estimated that 29.6% of Republicans report supporting political violence, while only 1.83% actually did.
Conversely, Republicans estimated that 19.5% of Democrats report supporting violence, while 3.54% actually did.
Thus, while both sides overestimated outparty political violence support, Democrats were significantly more pessimistic.
Study 2 replicated this effect in a nationally representative sample and found no similar asymmetry for nonpolitical crime or ingroup violence support.
Study 3 replicated the effect and showed that cognitive availability mediates perceived outparty violence support.
Study 4 found a similar, smaller asymmetry among Indian N.D.A. and I.N.D.I.A. alliance supporters.
These findings suggest that partisan misperceptions of political violence are asymmetric and partially arise from the cognitive availability of violent outgroup exemplars.

Scholars and the general public have become increasingly concerned about political violence, and in the US, many Americans believe the country is moving towards a civil war (1, 2) where disagreements will be resolved via violence (3).
text.formatted: Scholars and the general public have become increasingly concerned about political violence, and in the US, many Americans believe the country is moving towards a civil war <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2)</ref> where disagreements will be resolved via violence <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(3)</ref>.

text.text: These fears are underpinned by recent increases in political violence led by extremists (4, 5).
text.formatted: These fears are underpinned by recent increases in political violence led by extremists <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5)</ref>.

text.text: Such extremists, namely individuals who support or are willing to engage in politically motivated violence, pose a substantial threat to democratic stability and public safety (4, (6) (7) (8) (9) (10) (11) (12).
text.formatted: Such extremists, namely individuals who support or are willing to engage in politically motivated violence, pose a substantial threat to democratic stability and public safety <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(6)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(7)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(8)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(9)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(10)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(11)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(12)</ref>.

text.text: However, while acts of political violence such as the January 6th Capitol attack or the recent assassination attempts on Donald Trump are highly salient, previous research shows few people engage in such violence (13) (14) (15).
text.formatted: However, while acts of political violence such as the January 6th Capitol attack or the recent assassination attempts on Donald Trump are highly salient, previous research shows few people engage in such violence <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(13)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(14)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(15)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, average levels of support for political violence are low and often overestimated, particularly among political outgroup members (16).
text.formatted: Moreover, average levels of support for political violence are low and often overestimated, particularly among political outgroup members <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(16)</ref>.

text.text: Correcting these outgroup misperceptions reduces partisans' own support for political violence, highlighting the importance of identifying exaggerated intergroup perceptions (16).
text.formatted: Correcting these outgroup misperceptions reduces partisans' own support for political violence, highlighting the importance of identifying exaggerated intergroup perceptions <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(16)</ref>.

text.text: Here, we examine (a) whether Democrats and Republicans differ in the magnitude of overestimation bias for political violence support, (b) which psychological mechanisms underlie these misperceptions, and (c) whether asymmetries in perceived violence support reflect unique features of the United States.
We do so focusing on partisans' views on how widespread support for political violence is among their ingroup and outgroup.
Prior work finds several Democrat-Republican asymmetries among politically-relevant domains (17).
text.formatted: Prior work finds several Democrat-Republican asymmetries among politically-relevant domains <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(17)</ref>.

text.text: For example, exposure to an outparty Twitter bot increased ideological polarization among Republicans but not Democrats (18).
text.formatted: For example, exposure to an outparty Twitter bot increased ideological polarization among Republicans but not Democrats <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(18)</ref>.

text.text: Democrats are significantly more likely to identify (19) and support removing false information on social media than Republicans (20).
text.formatted: Democrats are significantly more likely to identify <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(19)</ref> and support removing false information on social media than Republicans <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(20)</ref>.

text.text: And insofar as Republicans are more conservative than Democrats (21) https://paperpile.com/c/nmfLz0/uWsqV available evidence suggests Republicans exhibit higher levels of authoritarianism, dogmatism, cognitive rigidity, need for certainty, social dominance orientation, sensitivity to elite polarization, and support for anti-democratic candidates or behaviors (22) (23) (24) (25).
text.formatted: And insofar as Republicans are more conservative than Democrats <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(21)</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://paperpile.com/c/nmfLz0/uWsqV">,</ref> available evidence suggests Republicans exhibit higher levels of authoritarianism, dogmatism, cognitive rigidity, need for certainty, social dominance orientation, sensitivity to elite polarization, and support for anti-democratic candidates or behaviors <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(22)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(23)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(24)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(25)</ref>.

text.text: Republicans are also less likely than Democrats to view democracy as the best form of government, and over half of Republicans agree that force may be required to save the traditional American way of life (compared to 22% of Democrats) (26).
text.formatted: Republicans are also less likely than Democrats to view democracy as the best form of government, and over half of Republicans agree that force may be required to save the traditional American way of life (compared to 22% of Democrats) <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(26)</ref>.

text.text: Republicans are also more likely to own guns than Democrats (27) https://paperpile.com/c/nmfLz0/wCX3h increasing Republicans' capacity for violent force.
text.formatted: Republicans are also more likely to own guns than Democrats <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(27)</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://paperpile.com/c/nmfLz0/wCX3h">,</ref> increasing Republicans' capacity for violent force.

text.text: But importantly, past findings suggest that Republicans, on average, do not exhibit higher levels of support for political violence than Democrats (16).
text.formatted: But importantly, past findings suggest that Republicans, on average, do not exhibit higher levels of support for political violence than Democrats <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(16)</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, Democrats' perceptions of outparty political violence support may be inflated by frequent portrayals of Republican aggression, particularly following January 6 th (28) (29) (30).
text.formatted: Nevertheless, Democrats' perceptions of outparty political violence support may be inflated by frequent portrayals of Republican aggression, particularly following January 6 th <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(28)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(29)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(30)</ref>.

text.text: Depictions of violent Republicans could make violent outparty exemplars highly salient and cognitively accessible to Democrats, who may then generalize to the larger outgroup.
These misperceptions may also reflect a view of Republicans as more capable of and more willing to use force to protect traditional values, even if doing so requires political violence.
Moreover, prior work finds that liberals exaggerate intergroup differences in moral concerns more than conservatives (31).
text.formatted: Moreover, prior work finds that liberals exaggerate intergroup differences in moral concerns more than conservatives <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(31)</ref>.

text.text: Based on these patterns, we hypothesize that Democrats will exhibit greater pessimism about how widespread Republicans' support for political violence is than vice versa.

Our hypothesis is further supported by recent data showing that Democrats are less likely to report having cross-party friendships (26) and are more geographically segregated than Republicans (32) https://paperpile.com/c/nmfLz0/aYgmc which may prevent natural corrections of inaccurate outparty perceptions (33).
text.formatted: Our hypothesis is further supported by recent data showing that Democrats are less likely to report having cross-party friendships <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(26)</ref> and are more geographically segregated than Republicans <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(32)</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://paperpile.com/c/nmfLz0/aYgmc">,</ref> which may prevent natural corrections of inaccurate outparty perceptions <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(33)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermorehttps://paperpile.com/c/nmfLz0/vfyZu Democrats may generalize from the highly salient subset of Republicans who are more supportive of political violence (34) , or Democrats' perceptions of the prevalence of political violence support may be biased by their views of Republican leaders as undemocratic.
text.formatted: Furthermore, Democrats may generalize from the highly salient subset of Republicans who are more supportive of political violence <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(34)</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://paperpile.com/c/nmfLz0/vfyZu">,</ref> or Democrats' perceptions of the prevalence of political violence support may be biased by their views of Republican leaders as undemocratic.

text.text: To evaluate this hypothesis, we collect data in three pre-registered studies (N=2,819)including two nationally representative samples-on partisans' support for political violence, as well as their perceptions and meta-perceptions about violent extremists in their own and opposing political parties.
In Study 2, we also assess respondents' concerns about ingroup and outgroup extremists and the possibility of a civil war.
In Study 3, we test potential mechanisms that may drive outgroup misperceptions of violence support.

Finally, to assess whether potential partisan asymmetries reflect unique features of the United States, we collect data in a fourth, pre-registered study (Study 4, N=620) on Indian partisans' support for political violence and their perceptions about outgroup members' support.
Our approach advances previous research in several crucial ways.
First, rather than focusing on average levels of support for political violence, we examine perceptions of how widespread support is.
Specifically, we asked participants to estimate the percentage of inparty and outparty members who will report supporting each action.

Doing so captures the extent to which individuals may perceive a widespread norm of political violence support among the outgroup, even when actual support may be concentrated among a small subset of extremists.

Secondhttps://paperpile.com/c/nmfLz0/aFFpu+oC1q2+rK6jT previous studies on Americans' support for political violence often lack specificity in defining the types of violence (4, 16, 35) , which can lead to ambiguity and inflated estimates of support (15).
text.formatted: Second, previous studies on Americans' support for political violence often lack specificity in defining the types of violence <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">35)</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://paperpile.com/c/nmfLz0/aFFpu+oC1q2+rK6jT">,</ref> which can lead to ambiguity and inflated estimates of support <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(15)</ref>.

text.text: By defining specific violent acts via vignettes, we aim to reduce this ambiguity and provide more accurate assessments.
Third, we explicitly test for an asymmetry between Democrats' and Republicans' perceptions of support for political violence.

Fourth, in Study 3, we experimentally manipulate exposure to violent or non-violent outparty exemplars to isolate causal mechanisms, assessing mediation via cognitive availability of violent outparty members, outparty-violence associations, and overall perceived outparty aggressiveness.
Fifth, in Study 4, we explore whether potential asymmetries in perceived support for violence can generalize beyond the United States.

In Study 1 (N = 408; US participants; pre-registered), as hypothesized, we find that although support for political violence is rare and overestimated among both parties, Democrats' outgroup perceptions were significantly more pessimistic than Republicans' (d = 0.34 for murder; d = 0.36 for assault; d = 0.39 for arson; all ps < .001) (see Figs. 1 and 2).
text.formatted: In Study 1 (N = 408; US participants; pre-registered), as hypothesized, we find that although support for political violence is rare and overestimated among both parties, Democrats' outgroup perceptions were significantly more pessimistic than Republicans' (d = 0.34 for murder; d = 0.36 for assault; d = 0.39 for arson; all ps < .001) (see Figs. <ref type="figure">1</ref> and <ref type="figure">2</ref>).

text.text: Across our three measures of political violence (i.e., murder, assault, and arson), Democrats, on average, predict that 29.60% of Republicans will report supporting political violence.
This exceeds the actual share of Republicans who report supporting political violence (1.83% averaged across our three measures) by 1,517%.
In contrast, Republicans predict that 19.48% of Democrats report supporting political violence.
This exceeds the actual share of Democrats who report supporting political violence (3.54%) by 450%.

These patterns emerge consistently across arson, assault with a deadly weapon, and murder, as Democrats' outgroup perceptions are approximately 10 percentage points higher than Republicans' outgroup perceptions on all three types of violence (see Fig. 1).
text.formatted: These patterns emerge consistently across arson, assault with a deadly weapon, and murder, as Democrats' outgroup perceptions are approximately 10 percentage points higher than Republicans' outgroup perceptions on all three types of violence (see Fig. <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: Democrats, on average, predict that 33.90% of Republicans will report supporting arson, that 29.42% of Republicans will report supporting assault with a deadly weapon, and that 25.49% of Republicans will report supporting murder.

In contrast, Republicans predict that 22.87% of Democrats will report supporting arson, that 19.51% of Democrats will report supporting assault with a deadly weapon, and that 16.05% of Democrats will report supporting murder.
Conversely, we do not find evidence that Democrats' average ingroup perceptions differ from Republicans' (p = .35).

Across our three measures of political violence, Democrats, on average, predict that 13.42% of other Democrats support political violence, while Republicans predict that 11.67% of other Republicans support political violence.

More specifically, Democrats, on average, predict that 17.81% of other Democrats will report supporting arson, that 12.45% of other Democrats will report supporting assault with a deadly weapon, and that 10.01% of other Democrats will report supporting murder.

Similarly, Republicans predict that 13.43% of other Republicans will report supporting arson, that 11.84% of other Republicans will report supporting assault with a deadly weapon, and that 9.76% of other Republicans will report supporting murder.
We also do not find evidence that actual reported support for political violence differs between Democrats and Republicans (all ps > .08).
text.formatted: We also do not find evidence that actual reported support for political violence differs between Democrats and Republicans (all ps > .08).

text.text: More specifically, 5.80% of Democrats report supporting arson compared to 1.99% of Republicans; 1.93% of Democrats report supporting assault with a deadly weapon compared to 2.49% of Republicans; and 2.90% of Democrats report supporting murder compared to 1.00% of Republicans.

Collectively, this suggests that the observed Democrat-Republican asymmetry is unique to intergroup perceptions rather than reflecting a broader difference in beliefs about how widespread political violence support is among most Americans or an underlying difference in actual reported political violence support.
To further explore asymmetries in perceived support for political violence, we examined Democrats' and Republicans' meta-perceptions (i.e., how one believes their group is perceived by others).

Our consideration of meta-perceptions is informed by previous findings that inaccurate meta-perceptions can contribute to polarization (36https://paperpile.com/c/nmfLz0/hc12y+6HGuV 37) https://paperpile.com/c/nmfLz0/hx9Za dehumanization (38) , and support for undemocratic practices (39).
text.formatted: Our consideration of meta-perceptions is informed by previous findings that inaccurate meta-perceptions can contribute to polarization <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(36,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">37)</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://paperpile.com/c/nmfLz0/hc12y+6HGuV">,</ref> dehumanization <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(38)</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://paperpile.com/c/nmfLz0/hx9Za">,</ref> and support for undemocratic practices <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(39)</ref>.

text.text: Given the observed asymmetry in perceptions of outgroup support for political violence, we expect Democrats to also hold more negative meta-perceptions than Republicans.
Indeed, we find evidence that Democrats' beliefs about what Republicans believe about them are too pessimistic (d = 0.56 for murder; d = 0.55 for assault; d = 0.61 for arson; all ps < .001).
text.formatted: Indeed, we find evidence that Democrats' beliefs about what Republicans believe about them are too pessimistic (d = 0.56 for murder; d = 0.55 for assault; d = 0.61 for arson; all ps < .001).

text.text: Democrats, on average, predicted Republicans would estimate that 35.25% of Democrats support political violence, nearly twice Republicans' actual prediction (19.48%).
By contrast, there are no significant differences between Republicans' metaperceptions and Democrats' actual outgroup perceptions (all ps > .16) (see Fig. S1).
text.formatted: By contrast, there are no significant differences between Republicans' metaperceptions and Democrats' actual outgroup perceptions (all ps > .16) (see Fig. <ref type="figure">S1</ref>).

text.text: Republicans, on average, predicted Democrats would estimate that 26.19% of Republicans support political violence, close to Democrats' actual prediction (29.60%).

This asymmetry is partially due to Democrats' meta-perceptions reflecting greater pessimism in absolute terms, not just relative to actual outgroup perceptions (d = 0.33 for murder; d = 0.29 for assault; d = 0.36 for arson; all ps < .005).
text.formatted: This asymmetry is partially due to Democrats' meta-perceptions reflecting greater pessimism in absolute terms, not just relative to actual outgroup perceptions (d = 0.33 for murder; d = 0.29 for assault; d = 0.36 for arson; all ps < .005).

text.text: These patterns are consistent across arson, assault, and murder (see SI and Fig. S1 for details).
text.formatted: These patterns are consistent across arson, assault, and murder (see SI and Fig. <ref type="figure">S1</ref> for details).

text.text: This suggests that-at least within the domain of political violence-Democrats hold more pessimistic views about how Republicans view Democrats than vice versa, potentially contributing to the observed Democrat-Republican asymmetry in predicted outgroup support for political violence.
To the extent that Democrats expect a higher share of Republicans to support political violence, Democrats may also be more concerned about politically violent outgroup extremists.

We investigate this possibility by measuring participants' levels of concern about ingroup and outgroup extremists (defined as those who support political violence) as threats to public safety, future election security, US democracy, and America.
We also assess concern via perceived importance of protecting against ingroup and outgroup extremists.
Finally, we examine the actual and perceived share of Democrats and Republicans who report concern about the possibility of a civil war occurring in the US.

We find that both Republicans and Democrats are more concerned about outgroup than ingroup extremists as threats to all four outcomes (all ps < .001 based on paired t-tests; see SI and Fig. S2 for details).
text.formatted: We find that both Republicans and Democrats are more concerned about outgroup than ingroup extremists as threats to all four outcomes (all ps < .001 based on paired t-tests; see SI and Fig. <ref type="figure">S2</ref> for details).

text.text: Yet, again, we find that Democrats are more concerned than Republicans about outgroup extremists as threats to public safety (M = 7.09, SD = 2.05 for Democrats; M = 6.63, SD = 2.45 for Republicans; d = 0.21, t(389) = 2.07, p = .039), future election security (M = 7.49, SD = 1.91 for Democrats; M = 6.83, SD = 2.39 for Republicans; d = 0.31, t(382) = 3.11, p = .002), US democracy (M = 7.55, SD = 1.84 for Democrats; M = 6.72, SD = 2.40 for Republicans; d = 0.39, t(375) = 3.90, p < .001), and America (M = 7.50, SD = 1.83 for Democrats; M = 6.85, SD = 2.43 for Republicans; d = 0.31, t(371) = 3.08, p = .002).
text.formatted: Yet, again, we find that Democrats are more concerned than Republicans about outgroup extremists as threats to public safety (M = 7.09, SD = 2.05 for Democrats; M = 6.63, SD = 2.45 for Republicans; d = 0.21, t(389) = 2.07, p = .039), future election security (M = 7.49, SD = 1.91 for Democrats; M = 6.83, SD = 2.39 for Republicans; d = 0.31, t(382) = 3.11, p = .002), US democracy (M = 7.55, SD = 1.84 for Democrats; M = 6.72, SD = 2.40 for Republicans; d = 0.39, t(375) = 3.90, p < .001), and America (M = 7.50, SD = 1.83 for Democrats; M = 6.85, SD = 2.43 for Republicans; d = 0.31, t(371) = 3.08, p = .002).

text.text: In contrast, we do not observe significant differences between Democrats' and Republicans' concerns about ingroup extremists (all ps > .13).
text.formatted: In contrast, we do not observe significant differences between Democrats' and Republicans' concerns about ingroup extremists (all ps > .13).

text.text: We observe a similar Democrat-Republican asymmetry in the perceived importance of protecting against outgroup extremists (see Fig. 2).
text.formatted: We observe a similar Democrat-Republican asymmetry in the perceived importance of protecting against outgroup extremists (see Fig. <ref type="figure">2</ref>).

text.text: Democrats rate protecting against outgroup extremists (M = 7.90, SD = 1.72) as significantly more important than Republicans do (M = 7.33, SD = 2.27; d = 0.29, t(373) = 2.88, p = .004).
As expected, this asymmetry does not emerge for protecting against ingroup extremists (M = 6.81, SD = 2.47 for Democrats; M = 7.04, SD = 2.44 for Republicans; t(406) = 0.96, p = .34).
Furthermore, only Democrats view protecting against outgroup extremists as significantly more important than protecting against ingroup extremists (t(206) = 6.77, p < .001).
text.formatted: Furthermore, only Democrats view protecting against outgroup extremists as significantly more important than protecting against ingroup extremists (t(206) = 6.77, p < .001).

text.text: Consistent with our previous findings, a greater share of Democrats (60.87%) expressed civil war concern than Republicans (49.75%) (𝛸𝛸 2 (1, N = 408) = 4.66, p = .031).

Furthermore, in contrast to perceptions of extremists, both Democrats and Republicans significantly underestimated the share of ingroup and outgroup members who are concerned about a potential civil war (all ps < .001; see SI and Fig. S3 for details).
text.formatted: Furthermore, in contrast to perceptions of extremists, both Democrats and Republicans significantly underestimated the share of ingroup and outgroup members who are concerned about a potential civil war (all ps < .001; see SI and Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">S3</ref> for details).

text.text: We also do not observe Democrat-Republican asymmetries in outgroup perceptions of civil war concern (M = 42.23, SD = 25.07 for Democrats; M = 40.57, SD = 25.07 for Republicans; t(406) = 0.67, p = .50), suggesting that the prior asymmetries do not simply reflect broad differences in intergroup perceptions but are instead specific to political violence.
In Study 2, we replicated our main results from Study 1 using a large sample that was nationally representative with respect to sex, age, and ethnicity (N = 906; US participants; pre-registered).

Given the consistency of responses across all three measures in Study 1, in Study 2, we measured support for political violence using only the murder vignette while omitting arson and deadly assault (see Methods for details).
We also included several additional measures to explore the boundaries of the observed Democrat-Republican asymmetry.
Specifically, we measured ingroup, outgroup, and meta-perceptions of affect.
We assessed the perceived prevalence of support for political violence among the most extreme ingroup and outgroup supporters, as well as among ingroup and outgroup leaders.
Additionally, we assessed participants' perceptions of whether typical outgroup members are more aggressive than typical ingroup members.
As a control measure, we examined reported and perceived support for drug trafficking, a non-politically-motivated crime.

We also included an alternative measure of levels of support for political violence used in previous studies (4, 16) and randomized whether participants saw this alternative measure before or after the vignette-based measures.
text.formatted: We also included an alternative measure of levels of support for political violence used in previous studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16)</ref> and randomized whether participants saw this alternative measure before or after the vignette-based measures.

text.text: Finally, we randomly assigned half of our participants to receive financial incentives for accuracy (40).
text.formatted: Finally, we randomly assigned half of our participants to receive financial incentives for accuracy <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(40)</ref>.

text.text: Replicating the main results of Study 1, we find that Democrats' outgroup perceptions of support for political violence are significantly more pessimistic than Republicans' (d = 0.23, p < .001), although both parties overestimate and rarely report support for political violence (see Figs. 3 and 4).
text.formatted: Replicating the main results of Study 1, we find that Democrats' outgroup perceptions of support for political violence are significantly more pessimistic than Republicans' (d = 0.23, p < .001), although both parties overestimate and rarely report support for political violence (see Figs. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">3</ref> and <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">4</ref>).

text.text: On average, Democrats predict that 22.57% of Republicans report supporting politically-motivated murder.
This exceeds the actual share of Republicans who report supporting politically-motivated murder (0.97%) by 2,227%.
Republicans on average predict that 16.90% of Democrats report supporting politicallymotivated murder.
This exceeds the actual share of Democrats who report supporting politically-motivated murder (1.42%) by 1,090%.
Again, we find no evidence that Democrats' ingroup perceptions of political violence support differ from Republicans' (d = 0.06, p = .36).
Democrats, on average, predict that 10.10% of other Democrats support political violence, while Republicans predict that 9.05% of other Republicans support political violence.
We also do not find evidence that reported support for political violence differs between Democrats and Republicans (𝛸𝛸 2 (1, N = 906) = 0.09, p = .760).
In Study 2, we complemented our vignette-based measure of support for political violence with an alternative, more abstract measure used in previous research (4, 16, 35, 41).
text.formatted: In Study 2, we complemented our vignette-based measure of support for political violence with an alternative, more abstract measure used in previous research <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">35,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">41)</ref>.

text.text: This alternative measure asks participants to rate their level of support for political violence using a 0-100 scale, rather than providing discrete choices.
Our findings suggest that the observed Democrat-Republican asymmetry appears consistently across both measures.

In contrast to prior work, we find Democrats are more pessimistic than Republicans about outgroup members, regardless of whether they responded to this abstract, alternative measure before (d = 0.44, p < .001) or after (d = 0.27, p = .004) the vignette-based measures.
text.formatted: In contrast to prior work, we find Democrats are more pessimistic than Republicans about outgroup members, regardless of whether they responded to this abstract, alternative measure before (d = 0.44, p < .001) or after (d = 0.27, p = .004) the vignette-based measures.

text.text: This suggests that the Democrat-Republican asymmetry can emerge even in the absence of a defined context for violence and provides evidence that Democrats may have relatively recently adopted a view of outgroup members as politically violent, regardless of how political violence is defined.
As in Study 1, we find evidence of a Democrat-Republican asymmetry in metaperceptions of politically-motivated violence support.
Democrats' beliefs about Republicans' outgroup perceptions are again too pessimistic (d = 0.57, p < .001).
text.formatted: Democrats' beliefs about Republicans' outgroup perceptions are again too pessimistic (d = 0.57, p < .001).

text.text: In contrast, we find only a marginal difference between Republicans' meta-perceptions and Democrats' outgroup perceptions (d = 0.13, p = .059) (see Fig. 4 and SI).
text.formatted: In contrast, we find only a marginal difference between Republicans' meta-perceptions and Democrats' outgroup perceptions (d = 0.13, p = .059) (see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">4</ref> and SI).

text.text: As in Study 1, we again find that this asymmetry is partially due to Democrats' meta-perceptions reflecting greater pessimism in absolute terms, not just relative to actual outgroup perceptions (d = 0.20, p = .003).
Democrats, on average, predicted Republicans would estimate that 31.01% of Democrats report supporting political violence, nearly twice Republicans' actual prediction (16.90%).
Republicans, on average, predicted Democrats would estimate that 25.78% of Republicans would report supporting political violence, slightly higher than Democrats' actual prediction (22.57%).

Replicating the results of Study 1, we find that Democrats are more concerned than Republicans about outparty extremists as threats to future election security (M = 7.53, SD = 1.98 for Democrats; M = 6.99, SD = 2.21 for Republicans; d = 0.26, t(833) = 3.86, p < .001), US democracy (M = 7.47, SD = 2.02 for Democrats; M = 6.92, SD = 2.32 for Republicans; d = 0.25, t(821) = 3.76, p < .001), and America (M = 7.36, SD = 2.02 for Democrats; M = 6.97, SD = 2.30 for Republicans; d = 0.18, t(824) = 2.65, p = .008).
text.formatted: Replicating the results of Study 1, we find that Democrats are more concerned than Republicans about outparty extremists as threats to future election security (M = 7.53, SD = 1.98 for Democrats; M = 6.99, SD = 2.21 for Republicans; d = 0.26, t(833) = 3.86, p < .001), US democracy (M = 7.47, SD = 2.02 for Democrats; M = 6.92, SD = 2.32 for Republicans; d = 0.25, t(821) = 3.76, p < .001), and America (M = 7.36, SD = 2.02 for Democrats; M = 6.97, SD = 2.30 for Republicans; d = 0.18, t(824) = 2.65, p = .008).

text.text: However, here Democrats are only marginally more concerned than Republicans about outgroup extremists as threats to public safety (M = 7.11, SD = 2.18 for Democrats; M = 6.85, SD = 2.38 for Republicans; d = 0.11, t(842) = 1.70, p = .090).
We again do not observe significant differences between Democrats' and Republicans' concern about ingroup extremists (all ps > .56).
text.formatted: We again do not observe significant differences between Democrats' and Republicans' concern about ingroup extremists (all ps > .56).

text.text: We also find that Republicans and Democrats are both more concerned about outgroup than ingroup extremists as threats to all four outcomes (all ps < .001 based on paired t-tests; see SI and Fig. S4 for details).
text.formatted: We also find that Republicans and Democrats are both more concerned about outgroup than ingroup extremists as threats to all four outcomes (all ps < .001 based on paired t-tests; see SI and Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">S4</ref> for details).

text.text: In contrast to Study 1, both Democrats and Republicans view protecting against outgroup extremists (M = 8.02, SD = 1.71 for Democrats; M = 7.60, SD = 2.07 for Republicans) as significantly more important than protecting against ingroup extremists (M = 7.17, SD = 2.52 for Democrats; M = 7.13, SD = 2.47 for Republicans; both ps < .001).
text.formatted: In contrast to Study 1, both Democrats and Republicans view protecting against outgroup extremists (M = 8.02, SD = 1.71 for Democrats; M = 7.60, SD = 2.07 for Republicans) as significantly more important than protecting against ingroup extremists (M = 7.17, SD = 2.52 for Democrats; M = 7.13, SD = 2.47 for Republicans; both ps < .001).

text.text: However, we again find that Democrats view protecting against outgroup extremists as significantly more important than Republicans (p = .001).
In Study 2, we also find that a majority of Democrats (53.04%) and Republicans (57.04%) report concern about the possibility of a civil war occurring in the US.

Replicating the results of Study 1, we do not observe Democrat-Republican asymmetries in the perceived share of outgroup or ingroup members who report concern about a potential civil war (both ps > .16).
text.formatted: Replicating the results of Study 1, we do not observe Democrat-Republican asymmetries in the perceived share of outgroup or ingroup members who report concern about a potential civil war (both ps > .16).

text.text: Both Democrats and Republicans also significantly underestimated the share of ingroup and outgroup members who report concern about a potential civil war (all ps < .001; see SI and Fig. S5).
text.formatted: Both Democrats and Republicans also significantly underestimated the share of ingroup and outgroup members who report concern about a potential civil war (all ps < .001; see SI and Fig. <ref type="figure">S5</ref>).

text.text: Why might Democrats show greater pessimism than Republicans about outparty support for political violence, and what is the scope of Democrat-Republican asymmetries?
We examine several related asymmetries to clarify the boundaries of this pattern.
First, we explore whether similar asymmetries exist for outparty affect (39, 42, 43).
text.formatted: First, we explore whether similar asymmetries exist for outparty affect <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(39,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">42,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">43)</ref>.

text.text: We find that, relative to Republicans, Democrats report more negative outgroup affect (M = 22.64, SD = 20.71 for Democrats; M = 32.47, SD = 25.12 for Republicans; d = -0.43, t(796) = -6.35, p < .001) and metaperceptions of affect (M = 18.43, SD = 17.76 for Democrats; M = 21.83, SD = 19.18 for Republicans; t(848) = -2.75, p = .006).
text.formatted: We find that, relative to Republicans, Democrats report more negative outgroup affect (M = 22.64, SD = 20.71 for Democrats; M = 32.47, SD = 25.12 for Republicans; d = -0.43, t(796) = -6.35, p < .001) and metaperceptions of affect (M = 18.43, SD = 17.76 for Democrats; M = 21.83, SD = 19.18 for Republicans; t(848) = -2.75, p = .006).

text.text: By contrast, Democrats do not feel more negative towards their ingroup than Republicans do (p = .462).

Second, we assess whether Democrats are more pessimistic than Republicans about the most extreme outgroup members' support for political violence, as these views could generalize to the outgroup or lead to extreme perceptions of the outgroup's behavioral norms (44).
text.formatted: Second, we assess whether Democrats are more pessimistic than Republicans about the most extreme outgroup members' support for political violence, as these views could generalize to the outgroup or lead to extreme perceptions of the outgroup's behavioral norms <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(44)</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with this explanation, when asked to imagine a group of the most extreme outgroup members, Democrats were significantly more pessimistic than Republicans about the share of extreme outgroup members who support political violence (M = 60.59, SD = 31.84 for Democrats; M = 46.74, SD = 35.00 for Republicans; d = 0.42, t(840) = 6.18, p < .001).
text.formatted: Consistent with this explanation, when asked to imagine a group of the most extreme outgroup members, Democrats were significantly more pessimistic than Republicans about the share of extreme outgroup members who support political violence (M = 60.59, SD = 31.84 for Democrats; M = 46.74, SD = 35.00 for Republicans; d = 0.42, t(840) = 6.18, p < .001).

text.text: That is, Democrats believed, on average, that 60.59% of the most extreme Republicans support political violence, whereas Republicans believed, on average, that 46.74% of the most extreme Democrats support political violence.
However, there was no such asymmetry for the most extreme ingroup members (p = .138).
Perceived Aggressiveness of Outgroup.
Third, Democrats may view Republicans as especially violent or aggressive in general, not just in political contexts.
To assess this possibility, we compare levels of agreement with the statement that the typical outgroup member is more aggressive than the typical ingroup member.

We find that Democrats endorse this statement significantly more than Republicans (M = 7.05, SD = 1.71 for Democrats; M = 6.05, SD = 2.30 for Republicans; d = 0.50, t(746) = 7.30, p < .001), suggesting that Democrats may perceive Republicans as more aggressive overall.
text.formatted: We find that Democrats endorse this statement significantly more than Republicans (M = 7.05, SD = 1.71 for Democrats; M = 6.05, SD = 2.30 for Republicans; d = 0.50, t(746) = 7.30, p < .001), suggesting that Democrats may perceive Republicans as more aggressive overall.

text.text: Perceptions and Reported Support for Non-Political Crime.
Fourth, Democrats may view Republicans as more supportive of crime generally.

We find that while support for non-political crime (i.e., drug trafficking) is also rare and overestimated, we do not observe a significant asymmetry between Democrats' and Republicans' outgroup predictions (M = 9.90, SD = 20.61 for Democrats; M = 12.31, SD = 20.53 for Republicans; d = -0.12, t(876) = -1.76, p = .080).

We also find evidence that the difference in Democrats' and Republicans' outgroup predictions is larger for politicallymotivated murder than for non-political crime, as there is a significant interaction between non-political crime and Republican party identification (d = -0.21, p < .001; see SI for details).
text.formatted: We also find evidence that the difference in Democrats' and Republicans' outgroup predictions is larger for politicallymotivated murder than for non-political crime, as there is a significant interaction between non-political crime and Republican party identification (d = -0.21, p < .001; see SI for details).

text.text: As expected, we do not find evidence of a Democrat-Republican asymmetry for ingroup predictions of drug trafficking support (d = 0.02, p = .796) (see Fig. 3).
text.formatted: As expected, we do not find evidence of a Democrat-Republican asymmetry for ingroup predictions of drug trafficking support (d = 0.02, p = .796) (see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">3</ref>).

text.text: These results-in combination with the observed asymmetry in outgroup aggressiveness-suggest that Democrats may perceive Republicans as specifically more violent (and thus supportive of political violence), rather than reflecting a generalized pessimism about Republicans' support for criminal behavior.
Views of Outgroup Leaders.
Fifth, we explore whether Democrats perceive more widespread support for political violence among outgroup leaders than Republicans.
That is, Democrats may view Republican leaders (e.g., Donald Trump) as more combative or supportive of violence than Republicans view Democrat leaders (e.g., Joe Biden and Kamala Harris).
This may negatively bias Democrats' perceptions and meta-perceptions while moderating Republicans'.

Yet, we find no significant asymmetry between Democrats' and Republicans' perceptions of outparty leaders' political violence support (M = 21.01, SD = 24.29 for Democrats; M = 18.39, SD = 26.95 for Republicans; d = 0.10, t(837) = 1.52, p = .128), suggesting that the observed asymmetries are not driven by generalized views about outparty politicians who use violent rhetoric or subvert democratic norms.

Notably, we also find that Republicans' perceptions of ingroup leaders are more negative than Democrats' (M = 6.65, SD = 14.02 for Democrats; M = 9.70, SD = 18.95 for Republicans; d = -0.19, t(743) = -2.71, p = .007).
Sixth, Democrats may exaggerate their stated outgroup perceptions to signal their political identity (45).
text.formatted: Sixth, Democrats may exaggerate their stated outgroup perceptions to signal their political identity <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(45)</ref>.

text.text: However, we find that providing financial incentives for accuracy has no significant effect on outgroup predictions among Democrats (d = 0.11, p = .223) or Republicans (d = -0.11, p = .267).
This suggests that respondents are reporting sincerely held beliefs rather than intentionally inflating their predictions to align with their political identity.
Together, these results help rule out expressive responding as an explanation for Democrats' heightened pessimism.

They also suggest that Democrats are not significantly more pessimistic about Republicans' support for all crime than vice versa, and we do not find evidence that Democrats are generalizing from their perceptions of outparty leaders.
Rather, the observed Democrat-Republican asymmetry may reflect generalizations from Democrats' views of extreme outgroup members and/or their overall views of Republicans as aggressive.

In Study 3 (N = 1,505; US participants; pre-registered), we replicated our main results from Studies 1 and 2 and tested whether exposure to a fictional violent or non-violent outparty exemplar causally impacts partisan misperceptions and meta-perceptions of political violence support (see Methods for details).
As in Study 2, our sample was nationally representative with respect to sex, age, and ethnicity.
In Study 3, we also examined whether any exemplar effects are mediated by availability-based processes, namely heightened cognitive accessibility of violent outparty members.
We additionally assessed associative and stereotype-based pathways, including strengthened outpartyviolence associations and increased beliefs about outparty aggressiveness, as potential mediators.

Replicating the main results of Studies 1 and 2, we find that Democrats' outgroup perceptions of support for political violence are significantly more pessimistic than Republicans' (d = 0.20, p < .001), although both parties overestimate outparty political violence support and themselves rarely report supporting political violence (see Figs. 5 and 6).
text.formatted: Replicating the main results of Studies 1 and 2, we find that Democrats' outgroup perceptions of support for political violence are significantly more pessimistic than Republicans' (d = 0.20, p < .001), although both parties overestimate outparty political violence support and themselves rarely report supporting political violence (see Figs. <ref type="figure">5</ref> and <ref type="figure">6</ref>).

text.text: On average, Democrats predict that 25.01% of Republicans report supporting politically-motivated murder.
This exceeds the actual share of Republicans who report supporting politically-motivated murder (1.06%) by 2,259%.
Republicans on average predict that 19.92% of Democrats report supporting politically-motivated murder.
This exceeds the actual share of Democrats who report supporting politically-motivated murder (1.33%) by 1,398%.
Again, we find no evidence that Democrats' ingroup perceptions of political violence support differ from Republicans' (d = 0.02, p = .66).
Democrats, on average, predict that 10.55% of other Democrats support political violence, while Republicans predict that 10.17% of other Republicans support political violence.
We also do not find evidence that reported support for political violence differs between Democrats and Republicans (𝛸𝛸 2 (1, N = 1,505) = 0.05, p = .815).
We next tested whether exposure to a violent or non-violent outparty exemplar affected perceptions of outgroup political violence support.
Overall, we find exposure to a violent exemplar increased perceived outparty support for political violence relative to a null control (b = 5.68, SE = 1.57, t(1499) = 3.61, p < .001, d = 0.23).
text.formatted: Overall, we find exposure to a violent exemplar increased perceived outparty support for political violence relative to a null control (b = 5.68, SE = 1.57, t(1499) = 3.61, p < .001, d = 0.23).

text.text: In contrast, exposure to a non-violent exemplar did not affect perceived outparty support relative to control (b = 1.71, SE = 1.58, t(1499) = 1.09, p = .523, d = 0.07).
Overall, participants in the violentexemplar condition estimated that 25.7% of outparty members report supporting politically motivated murder (vs.
20.0% in control; 21.7% in the non-violent condition).

There was no significant Condition × Party interaction (ps > .687), but simple-effects analyses indicated that the violent-exemplar effect was significant among Democrats (b = 6.31, SE = 2.23, t(1499) = 2.84, p = .013, d = 0.24) and not significant among Republicans (b = 5.05, SE = 2.23, t(1499) = 2.26, p = .061, d = 0.21).
text.formatted: There was no significant Condition × Party interaction (ps > .687), but simple-effects analyses indicated that the violent-exemplar effect was significant among Democrats (b = 6.31, SE = 2.23, t(1499) = 2.84, p = .013, d = 0.24) and not significant among Republicans (b = 5.05, SE = 2.23, t(1499) = 2.26, p = .061, d = 0.21).

text.text: Comparing across conditions, we find that exposure to a violent outparty exemplar brought Republicans' estimates in line with Democrats' baseline perceptions.
Democrats in the control condition predicted that 22.25% of Republicans support politically motivated murder.
Republicans exposed to a violent outparty exemplar predicted that 22.81% of Democrats support politically motivated murder (b = -0.56, SE = 2.23, t(1499) = -0.25, p = .801).

This pattern suggests that previously observed Democrat-Republican asymmetries in perceived outparty violence support may partly reflect differential availability of extreme outparty exemplars, rather than stable partisan differences in pessimism.

Notably, however, Democrats exposed to a violent exemplar further increased their estimates of outparty members' support for political violence, underscoring that exemplar-driven salience can amplify pessimism across both parties.
What psychological processes underlie the effect of violent exemplars on perceptions of outgroup support for political violence?

We tested three preregistered mechanisms: (1) heightened cognitive availability of violent outparty members, (2) stronger associative links between the outparty and violence, and (3) generalized beliefs about outparty aggressiveness.
As preregistered, we first estimated separate single-mediator models to test whether each pathway independently accounted for exemplar effects.

We find a significant indirect effect of cognitive availability of violent outparty members on partisans' perceptions of outgroup support for political violence (ACME = 0.06, 95% CI [0.02, 0.10], p = .007).
We also find a significant direct effect (ADE = 0.17, 95% CI [0.05, 0.28], p = .003) and total effect (0.23, 95% CI [0.10, 0.35], p < .001).
text.formatted: We also find a significant direct effect (ADE = 0.17, 95% CI [0.05, 0.28], p = .003) and total effect (0.23, 95% CI [0.10, 0.35], p < .001).

text.text: The indirect effect mediated approximately 26.4% of the total effect.

We also find a significant indirect effect of generalized beliefs about outparty aggressiveness on partisans' perceptions of outgroup support for political violence (ACME = 0.05, 95% CI [0.01, 0.09], p = .018).
We also find a significant direct effect (ADE = 0.18, 95% CI [0.06, 0.29], p = .005) and total effect (0.22, 95% CI [0.04, 0.50], p = .019).
The indirect effect mediated approximately 21.6% of the total effect.

By contrast, although there was a directionally similar effect of associative strength between violence and the outparty, the indirect effect did not reach statistical significance (ACME = 0.06, 95% CI [-0.00, 0.11], p = .055).
There was a significant direct effect (ADE = 0.17, 95% CI [0.06, 0.28], p = .002) and total effect (0.23, 95% CI [0.10, 0.35], p < .001).
text.formatted: There was a significant direct effect (ADE = 0.17, 95% CI [0.06, 0.28], p = .002) and total effect (0.23, 95% CI [0.10, 0.35], p < .001).

text.text: As pre-registered, we then fit a serial mediation model to assess whether violent exemplars increased accessibility of violent outparty representations, which in turn heightened perceived outparty aggressiveness and increased perceived outparty violence support.

We find evidence consistent with a significant indirect pathway (0.04, 95% CI [0.01, 0.07], z = 2.78, p = .005), suggesting that exposure to a violent outparty exemplar increases perceptions of outgroup violence support, in part, by elevating the cognitive accessibility of violent exemplars and, subsequently, perceived outparty aggressiveness.

These results are consistent with patterns observed within the control condition, as Democrats (relative to Republicans) reported more pessimistic perceptions of outgroup political violence support (d = 0.19, p = .033), higher cognitive availability of violent outparty members (d = 0.48, p < .001), beliefs that outparty members were more aggressive (d = 0.48, p < .001), and greater associative strength between violence and the outparty (d = 0.41, p < .001).

text.text: As in Studies 1 and 2, we find evidence of a Democrat-Republican asymmetry in metaperceptions of politically-motivated violence support.
Democrats' beliefs about Republicans' outgroup perceptions are again too pessimistic (d = 0.59, p < .001).

text.text: In contrast, we find no significant difference between Republicans' meta-perceptions and Democrats' outgroup perceptions (d = 0.01, p = .785) (see Fig. 6 and SI).

text.text: As in Studies 1 and 2, we again find that this asymmetry is partially due to Democrats' meta-perceptions reflecting greater pessimism in absolute terms, not just relative to actual outgroup perceptions (d = 0.37, p < .001).

text.text: Democrats, on average, predicted Republicans would estimate that 34.98% of Democrats report supporting political violence, significantly higher than Republicans' actual prediction (19.92%).
Republicans, on average, predicted Democrats would estimate that 25.37% of Republicans would report supporting political violence, close to Democrats' actual prediction (25.01%).
We next tested whether exposure to a violent or non-violent outparty exemplar affected meta-perceptions of political violence support.

We find no evidence that either violent or non-violent exemplars shifted meta-perceptions relative to the control condition (violent vs. control: b = 2.57, SE = 1.65, t(1499) = 1.56, p = .263; non-violent vs. control: b = 0.32, SE = 1.65, t(1499) = 0.20, p = .979).
These effects did not differ by party (all Condition × Party ps > .980).
text.formatted: These effects did not differ by party (all Condition × Party ps > .980).

text.text: Thus, whereas violent exemplars increased perceptions of outparty violence support, they did not meaningfully shift beliefs about how one's own group is viewed by the outparty.
In Study 3, we replicate several of the additional Democrat-Republican asymmetries found in Study 2.

More specifically, we again find that relative to Republicans, Democrats report more negative outgroup affect (M = 19.92, SD = 21.89 for Democrats; M = 36.39, SD = 24.70 for Republicans; d = -0.71, t(1481) = -13.69, p < .001) and meta-perceptions of affect (M = 19.21, SD = 17.97 for Democrats; M = 26.14, SD = 21.04 for Republicans; d = -0.35, t(1467) = -6.87, p < .001).

text.text: By contrast, Democrats do not feel more negative towards their ingroup than Republicans do (p = .105).

As in Study 2, we find Democrats were significantly more pessimistic than Republicans about the share of extreme outgroup members who support political violence (M = 56.72, SD = 33.34 for Democrats; M = 41.99, SD = 33.18 for Republicans; d = 0.44, t(1503) = 8.59, p < .001).

However, there was only a marginal asymmetry for the most extreme ingroup members (p = .070).

Replicating Study 2, we do not find a significant asymmetry between Democrats' and Republicans' outgroup predictions of support for non-political crime (i.e., drug trafficking) (M = 12.24, SD = 22.71 for Democrats; M = 13.54, SD = 20.39 for Republicans; d = -0.06, t(1486) = -1.18, p = .240).

We also find evidence that the difference in Democrats' and Republicans' outgroup predictions is larger for politicallymotivated murder than for non-political crime, as there is a significant interaction between non-political crime and Republican party identification (d = -0.29, p < .001; see SI for details).

In Study 3, we also find that a majority of Democrats (58.96%) and many Republicans (42.82%) report concern about the possibility of a civil war occurring in the US.

In Study 4 (N = 620; Indian participants; pre-registered), we examined whether the main results from Studies 1-3 can generalize beyond the United States by testing for a similar asymmetry between supporters of India's two major political alliances: the N.D.A. alliance and the I.N.D.I.A. alliance.
As expected, I.N.D.I.A. supporters identified as significantly more left ideologically than N.D.A. supporters on a 0 (left) to 10 (right) scale (M = 5.02 vs.
As in Studies 2 and 3, we measured support for political violence using the murder vignette and support for nonpolitical crime using the drug trafficking vignette.

We additionally measured affect, perceptions of outgroup and ingroup leaders' support for violence, and perceptions of the most extreme outgroup and ingroup members' support for violence (see Methods for details).

As in Studies 2 and 3, I.N.D.I.A. supporters were also significantly more pessimistic than N.D.A. supporters about the share of extreme outgroup members who support political violence (M = 53.74, SD = 33.48 for I.N.D.I.A. supporters; M = 45.35, SD = 34.03 for N.D.A. supporters; d = 0.25, t(615) = 3.09, p = .002).

That is, I.N.D.I.A. supporters believed, on average, that 53.74% of the most extreme N.D.A. supporters support political violence, whereas N.D.A. supporters believed, on average, that 45.35% of the most extreme I.N.D.I.A. supporters support political violence.

However, there was no such asymmetry for the most extreme ingroup members (M = 43.77, SD = 31.51 for I.N.D.I.A. supporters; M = 42.44, SD = 33.91 for N.D.A. supporters; d = 0.04, t(608) = 0.50, p = .615).

Unlike in Studies 2 and 3, we also do not find that I.N.D.I.A. supporters view the outgroup as more aggressive than N.D.A. supporters do.

Agreement with the statement that the typical outgroup member is more aggressive than the typical ingroup member did not differ between I.N.D.I.A. supporters (M = 6.01, SD = 2.45) and N.D.A. supporters (M = 5.95, SD = 2.35; d = 0.02, t(609) = 0.31, p = .760).
Thus, here the asymmetry in outgroup perceptions of political violence support emerged even in the absence of asymmetries in affect or in general beliefs about the outgroup's aggressiveness.
We conducted four pre-registered studies (N=3,439) focused on U.S. partisans (Studies 1-3) and Indian partisans (Study 4).

In Studies 1-3, we provide evidence that reported support for political violence is rare, and both Democrats and Republicans significantly overestimate the prevalence of reported political violence support.
Critically, across three studies and several outcomes, we find that Democrats exhibit greater pessimism towards Republicans' reported support for political violence than vice versa.

This asymmetry emerged consistently across different types of political violence (Study 1), across different measurement formats (Study 2), across multiple nationally representative samples collected over a year apart (Studies 2 and 3), and across both the United States and India (Studies 1-4).
What might drive this asymmetry?
Study 3 offers experimental evidence that exposure to a single (fictional) violent outparty exemplar causally increases perceived outparty support for political violence.
Moreover, exposing Republicans to a violent outparty exemplar increased their estimates to match Democrats' baseline perceptions in the control condition.

Mediation analyses reveal that the effect of violent exemplars operated through increased cognitive availability of violent outparty members, which in turn elevated beliefs about outparty aggressiveness and support for violence.

This suggests that a vivid and extreme example of a violent outparty member can make similar instances of violent outparty members more cognitively available, leading partisans to overgeneralize the prevalence of such support within the outgroup.
Similarly, within the control condition, we find evidence that violent outparty exemplars were more cognitively available to Democrats than Republicans.

These findings align with availability-based accounts of social judgment (46) (47) (48) and provide the first evidence, to our knowledge, identifying psychological processes underlying inflated political misperceptions.

text.text: We note that Democrats exposed to a violent exemplar also increased their estimates of outparty political violence support relative to control, indicating that the observed partisan asymmetry does not reflect a rigid baseline bias among Democrats.
Both Democrats and Republicans responded to a salient violent exemplar.

In light of past work showing that partisans are often exposed to information that reinforces negative stereotypes of the outgroup (https://paperpile.com/c/nmfLz0/KMBLf with Democrats potentially encountering more portrayals of Republican aggression (28) particularly following January 6th (29https://paperpile.com/c/nmfLz0/8a73I+9ptTB 30) , our findings suggest that the observed Democrat-Republican asymmetry may reflect different informational environments (50) (51) (52).

text.text: We do not find evidence that exposure to a non-violent outparty exemplar affects perceived outparty support for political violence among either Democrats or Republicans.
This pattern suggests that partisans are not simply considering any outparty exemplar and assessing that exemplar's likely attitudes toward violence.

Rather, it seems partisans specifically attempt to retrieve or imagine a violent outparty exemplar and then infer broader support for political violence based on how readily that exemplar comes to mind.
The ease of accessing such an example (i.e., its cognitive availability) appears to shape perceptions of how widespread violent attitudes are within the outgroup.
Additionally, meta-perceptions were largely unaffected by the manipulation, suggesting that beliefs about how one's own group is viewed by the outparty may be less malleable to isolated exemplars.
Study 4 indicates that this asymmetry is not unique to the United States.
Among Indian partisans, supporters of the relatively left-leaning I.N.D.I.A. alliance were more pessimistic than N.D.A. alliance supporters about outgroup members' support for political violence.
Our findings extend prior research indicating that Americans often misperceive political outgroup members' attitudes (16).
text.formatted: Our findings extend prior research indicating that Americans often misperceive political outgroup members' attitudes <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(16)</ref>.

text.text: In addition to identifying cognitive availability of violent exemplars as a key mechanism, our work is the first to demonstrate a partisan asymmetry in outgroup perceptions of the prevalence of political violence support, and we find evidence of a similar asymmetry among Indian partisans.
Notably, across all four studies, we do not observe a significant asymmetry in ingroup perceptions of support for political violence.

We also do not observe a Democrat-Republican asymmetry in outgroup members' support for non-political crimes such as drug trafficking, and the asymmetry was significantly larger for political violence than for drug trafficking in Studies 2 and 3.
This suggests that, among U.S. partisans, Democrats' heightened pessimism is specific to perceptions of reported political violence support among outgroup members.

Research on partisan misperceptions indicates that such specificity may reflect the perceived danger of political violence relative to other issues, as individuals often perceive greater partisan differences among issues they consider important (53, 54).
text.formatted: Research on partisan misperceptions indicates that such specificity may reflect the perceived danger of political violence relative to other issues, as individuals often perceive greater partisan differences among issues they consider important <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(53,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">54)</ref>.

text.text: Beyond cognitive availability, other factors may partially contribute to the Democrat-Republican asymmetry in outgroup perceptions of political violence support.
Democrats reported more negative affect toward Republicans and more negative affective meta-perceptions.
Thus, Democrats' pessimism toward Republicans' political violence support may partially reflect highly negative outgroup attitudes.
This is consistent with our finding that Democrats also believed that Republicans viewed them as more likely to report supporting political violence than vice versa.

However, affective differences do not appear to be strictly necessary for the asymmetry to emerge: in Study 4, I.N.D.I.A. supporters were more pessimistic than N.D.A. supporters about outgroup members' support for political violence even though the two groups did not differ in outgroup affect or affective meta-perceptions.

Likewise, I.N.D.I.A. supporters held more pessimistic meta-perceptions of drug trafficking support despite no asymmetry in outgroup predictions for that crime, suggesting that more pessimistic meta-perceptions need not accompany more pessimistic outgroup perceptions.
Future research should explore the extent to which these variables are causally linked.

Additionally, Democrats perceived the most extreme Republicans as more supportive of political violence than vice versa (Studies 2 and 3), and I.N.D.I.A. supporters showed the same pattern for the most extreme N.D.A. supporters (Study 4).

Democrats may generalize from the actions or rhetoric of a salient subset of Republicans who seemingly endorse political violence (34) https://paperpile.com/c/nmfLz0/vfyZu which increases Democrats' overall outgroup misperceptions about the pervasiveness of political violence support.

text.text: Importantly, we note that these asymmetries may also reflect actual differences in political violence support among extreme Republicans and Democrats rather than biased intergroup processes on behalf of the average Democrat.

Past research suggests that a subset of Republicans -namely Trump supporters who deny the validity of the 2020 electionare significantly more likely than other groups to support political violence (34).

text.text: While prior work has not found partisan asymmetries in perceived outgroup violence support (16, 39), the continued visibility of these subgroups and of Donald Trump in recent public discourse may render extreme Republican exemplars more cognitively accessible to Democrats.
text.formatted: While prior work has not found partisan asymmetries in perceived outgroup violence support <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">39)</ref>, the continued visibility of these subgroups and of Donald Trump in recent public discourse may render extreme Republican exemplars more cognitively accessible to Democrats.

text.text: This heightened salience could help explain the asymmetry observed in our studies.

Nevertheless, given the low levels of political violence support observed among both U.S. parties, such perceptions of widespread self-reported support for political violence among outgroup members are likely misrepresentative of reality.

However, we do not find evidence that the observed Democrat-Republican asymmetry simply captures participants' exaggerating their stated perceptions, as providing financial incentives for accuracy did not significantly affect Democrats' or Republicans' outgroup predictions.
This suggests that the observed Democrat-Republican asymmetries reflect genuine differences in outgroup perception.
Our findings are subject to several limitations.
Here, we have focused on an online sample of self-identified Democrats and Republicans (Studies 1-3) and I.N.D.I.A. and N.D.A. alliance supporters (Study 4).
Although Studies 2 and 3 use samples that are demographically representative of the U.S., online samples may differ from real-world populations.
Similarly, although Study 4 uses a sample that is nationally representative with respect to politics, we relied on English-speaking participants who may differ from non-English speakers.
Future research could explore the generalizability of this asymmetry among non-English speakers, as well as among other countries beyond the United States and India.
Additionally, we rely on self-report data, which may be subject to social desirability bias, especially given the sensitivity of political violence support.
Future research could, therefore, incorporate implicit measures and behavioral indicators to corroborate self-reported attitudes.
Finally, partisans' tendency to overestimate the proportion of others, even inparty members, who support political violence may partially reflect general numeracy biases in cognition (55).
text.formatted: Finally, partisans' tendency to overestimate the proportion of others, even inparty members, who support political violence may partially reflect general numeracy biases in cognition <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(55)</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, these findings identify a consistent partisan asymmetry: Democrats perceive Republicans as more supportive of political violence than vice versa.

This asymmetry holds across various forms of violence (Study 1) and measurement formats (Study 2), and is accompanied by Democrats expressing greater concern about outgroup extremists, more negative affect and meta-perceptions, and stronger beliefs in Republican aggressiveness (Studies 1-3).
A similar asymmetry emerged among Indian partisans (Study 4), as I.N.D.I.A. supporters were more pessimistic than N.D.A. supporters about outgroup members.
Study 3 identifies a causal mechanism underlying such partisan misperceptions.
Exposure to a single violent outparty exemplar increased perceived outparty support for violence via heightened cognitive availability and, in turn, aggressiveness perceptions.

This exposure eliminated the partisan gap by raising Republicans' estimates to match Democrats', suggesting that asymmetric exposure to violent outparty exemplars may help sustain real-world misperception gaps.
More broadly, these findings underscore the importance of tailoring interventions to different populations.

Interventions aimed at correcting inflated beliefs about widespread outparty support for political violence may be especially impactful among Democrats and I.N.D.I.A. alliance supporters, whereas approaches targeting Republicans and N.D.A. alliance supporters may need to address other dimensions of partisan conflict.

At the same time, our results highlight the risks of interventions or public discourse that emphasize extreme outparty actors: even a single salient exemplar was sufficient to elevate perceived outparty support for violence and erase baseline partisan differences.

Thus, efforts to reduce misperceptions may be undermined by media environments, political rhetoric, or communication strategies that foreground extreme cases, inadvertently amplifying perceived threat.

Promoting accurate beliefs about the true prevalence of political violence support while avoiding disproportionate focus on rare but dramatic instances may therefore be critical to reducing partisan fear and fostering a healthier democratic environment.
