text.text: All remaining participants were included in the analyses (N = 408; 207 Democrats, 201 Republicans; 203 female; Mage = 38.6, SDage = 13.3).

To measure support for political violence, participants read each of the following vignettes, adapted from prior literature (https://paperpile.com/c/nmfLz0/nQd9U and were asked: "Do you support or oppose [name's] actions?"
text.formatted: To measure support for political violence, participants read each of the following vignettes, adapted from prior literature (<ref type="url" target="https://paperpile.com/c/nmfLz0/nQd9U">15),</ref> and were asked: "Do you support or oppose [name's] actions?"

text.text: Responses included "Support," "Neither support nor oppose," and "Oppose."
Arson: "[name] was convicted of arson.

He was arrested by police after starting a fire at the local [outgroup] Party's headquarters. [name] targeted the headquarters because he believed that the [outgroup] Party is harmful to the nation's future."
Assault with a deadly weapon: "[name] was convicted of assault with a deadly weapon.
He was arrested by police after driving his car into a crowd of [outgroup] protesters.

Although no one was killed, several individuals were seriously injured and one spent a month in the hospital. [name] targeted the victims because he believed that the [outgroup] Party is harmful to the nation's future."
Murder: "[name] was convicted of murder.
He was arrested by police after stabbing a prominent [outgroup] to death. [name] targeted the victim because he believed that the [outgroup] Party is harmful to the nation's future."
To measure perceptions of their outgroup/ingroup, participants were instructed, "Please indicate what percentage of [outgroup/ingroup] you believe will support [name's] actions.
(Please use a number from 0 to 100, decimals allowed.)."
To measure meta-perceptions, participants were told, "We are asking [outgroup] to predict what percentage of [ingroup] will support [name's] actions.
text.formatted: To measure meta-perceptions, participants were told, "We are asking <ref type="bibr">[outgroup]</ref> to predict what percentage of [ingroup] will support [name's] actions.

text.text: What do you think the average [outgroup]'s prediction will be?
(Please use a number from 0 to 100, decimals allowed.)"

To minimize potential confusion, participants received the following example: "For example, if you think that the average [outgroup] will predict that half of all [ingroup] would support [name's] actions, you would enter "50"."

To measure concern about outgroup/ingroup extremists, participants were asked to "Please take a moment to think about [outgroup] who support or are willing to engage in politically-motivated violence like the actions you just read.
On a scale from 1 to 9, how much of a threat do you think these [outgroup/ingroup] pose to each of the following?"

Participants responded using a 9-point scale ranging from "Not a threat at all" to "Extreme threat" for each of the following outcomes: Public Safety, Future Election Security, US Democracy, and America.

As an additional measure of concern, participants were asked, "On a scale from 1 to 9, how important do you think it is to protect against [outgroup/ingroup] who support or are willing to engage in politically-motivated violence?"
Participants responded using a 9point scale ranging from "Not at all important" to "Extremely important."
To measure concern about civil war, participants were asked, "Are you concerned about the possibility of a civil war occurring in the United States?"
Participants responded with a dichotomous "Yes" or "No."

To measure outgroup/ingroup perceptions about civil war concern, participants were asked to "Please indicate what percentage of [outgroup/ingroup] you believe are concerned about the possibility of civil war in the United States.
(Please use a number from 0 to 100, decimals allowed.)."
Finally, as an attention check, participants were asked, "What was NOT covered in this study?"
with the following randomly-ordered response options: Murder, Setting Fire, Driving a car into a crowd, Crashing a plane.
Participants who did not select "Crashing a plane" were excluded from all analyses.
Study 2 used a large representative sample (N = 1,589) recruited from Prolific during 08/22/2024 -08/26/2024.

As pre-registered (https://researchbox.org/4077&PEER_REVIEW_passcode=VXOCYQ), we excluded 674 participants who did not identify as either "Republican" or "Democrat" and 8 participants who failed an attention check.
text.formatted: As pre-registered (<ref type="url" target="https://researchbox.org/4077&PEER_REVIEW_passcode=VXOCYQ">https://researchbox.org/4077&PEER_REVIEW_passcode=VXOCYQ</ref>), we excluded 674 participants who did not identify as either "Republican" or "Democrat" and 8 participants who failed an attention check.

text.text: We also excluded 1 participant whose responses included impossible values (e.g., predicting that 500% of outgroup members support drug trafficking).
All remaining participants were included in the analyses (N = 906; 494 Democrats, 412 Republicans; 450 female; Mage = 46.9, SDage = 16.1).
As noted above, given the consistency of responses across all three measures in Study 1, in Study 2, we measured support for political violence using only the murder vignette.
We also used the following vignette to explore misperceptions for a non-politicallymotivated, non-violent crime (drug trafficking): Drug Trafficking: "[name] was convicted of drug trafficking.
He was arrested by police after transporting large quantities of heroin into local neighborhoods.
[name] targeted these areas because he believed that the demand for drugs would ensure him massive personal financial profits, regardless of the drugs' harmfulness."
Participants' own support and ingroup, outgroup, and meta-perceptions were measured using identical procedures to Study 1.
However, in Study 2, we randomly assigned half of our participants to receive financial incentives for accuracy (40).
text.formatted: However, in Study 2, we randomly assigned half of our participants to receive financial incentives for accuracy <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(40)</ref>.

text.text: Participants assigned to receive accuracy incentives read the following instructions prior to making predictions about the outgroup: "You will earn a 50 cent bonus ($0.50) if your predictions are, on average, within 5 percentage points of the true value."

To measure concern about outgroup/ingroup extremists, participants were asked to "Please take a moment to think about [outgroup] who support or are willing to engage in politically-motivated violence like stabbing a prominent political figure to death."
Otherwise, the procedures used to measure concern were identical to Study 1.
Perceived importance of protecting against extremists and civil war concern were also measured using the same procedures as Study 1.
In Study 2, we added measures of perceived support for political violence among outgroup and ingroup leaders (e.g., elected officials), as well as among the most extreme outgroup and ingroup members.

To measure perceptions of outgroup and ingroup leaders, participants were instructed, "We are also interested in how you think leaders of the [outgroup/ingroup] Party (e.g., elected officials) would respond to similar questions.
Please indicate what percentage of [outgroup/ingroup] leaders you believe will support [name's] actions.
(Please use a number from 0 to 100, decimals allowed.)."
To measure perceptions of the most extreme outgroup and ingroup members, participants were instructed, "Now, imagine a group of the most extreme [outparty/inparty] supporters.
Please indicate what percentage of the most extreme [outgroup/ingroup] supporters you believe will support [name's] actions.
(Please use a number from 0 to 100, decimals allowed.)."

We also assessed participants' perceptions of whether typical outgroup members are more aggressive than typical ingroup members using the following: "To what extent do you agree or disagree with the statement: The typical [outgroup] is more aggressive than the typical [ingroup]. "1" means "Strongly disagree" and "9" means "Strongly agree."
We also included an alternative measure of support for political violence used in previous studies (16, 41).
text.formatted: We also included an alternative measure of support for political violence used in previous studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">41)</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, we ask (1) how much participants feel it is justified for [ingroup] to use violence in advancing their political goals these days, and (2) how much participants feel it is justified for [ingroup] to use violence if the [outgroup] Party wins the next presidential election.
Responses for both items range from 0 ("Never") to 100 ("Always") (16).
text.formatted: Responses for both items range from 0 ("Never") to 100 ("Always") <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(16)</ref>.

text.text: Participants then predicted the average ingroup and outgroup members' responses.

Given ongoing debates regarding whether measures that contain ambiguous definitions of violence can meaningfully capture support for political violence (15), we randomly assigned half of our participants-stratified by political party-to respond to these alternative measures before the vignette-based measure.
We also measured ingroup, outgroup, and meta-perceptions of affect using standard feeling thermometers (42, 43).
text.formatted: We also measured ingroup, outgroup, and meta-perceptions of affect using standard feeling thermometers <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(42,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">43)</ref>.

text.text: See SI for additional details.
Finally, as an attention check, participants were asked, "What was NOT covered in this study?"
with the following randomly-ordered response options: Murder, Selling drugs, Civil war, and Crashing a plane.
Participants who did not select "Crashing a plane" were excluded from all analyses.
We recruited a large representative sample (N = 1,556) from Prolific during 10/23/2025 -10/27/2025.

As pre-registered (https://osf.io/muq59/overview?view_only=7093bebefbb34b5bb78b4d10e17d18df), we excluded 37 participants who did not identify as either "Republican" or "Democrat" and 14 participants who failed an attention check.
text.formatted: As pre-registered (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/muq59/overview?view_only=7093bebefbb34b5bb78b4d10e17d18df">https://osf.io/muq59/overview?view_only=7093bebefbb34b5bb78b4d10e17d18df</ref>), we excluded 37 participants who did not identify as either "Republican" or "Democrat" and 14 participants who failed an attention check.

text.text: All remaining participants were included in the analyses (N = 1,505; 753 Democrats, 752 Republicans; 749 female; Mage = 45.7, SDage = 14.5).
Participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: exposure to a violent outparty exemplar, exposure to a non-violent outparty exemplar, or a pure control (no exemplar).
In the two exemplar conditions, participants read a short description of an outparty member named "Bob" accompanied by a simple cartoon image.
In the violent exemplar condition, Bob was described as follows: "Bob is a [Democrat/Republican] and an active member of radical political groups.
He feels constant anger about politics and believes that confrontation is necessary to defend his values.
Bob often attends heated political rallies where fights break out, and he has engaged in violent behavior during these events.
People describe him as intense, confrontational, quick-tempered, and driven by outrage."
In the non-violent exemplar condition, Bob was described as follows: "Bob is a [Democrat/Republican] and [works as a high school teacher/owns a family farm].
He loves spending time with his wife and kids, often coaching his son's soccer team on weekends.
He believes strongly in promoting fairness and social responsibility, but he is careful to respect rules and order.
Bob is calm, dependable, and has never harmed anyone.
He's known in his community as someone who can always be trusted to do the right thing."
Participants in either exemplar condition then rated how "typical" Bob was of the outparty (1-9 scale, "Not at all typical" to "Very typical").
We assessed three preregistered mechanisms.

Cognitive availability of violent outparty members was measured by participants' level of agreement or disagreement with the statement, "It is easy for me to think of violent [Democrats/Republicans]" (1-9 scale, "Strongly disagree" to "Strongly agree").

Associative strength between violence and the outparty was measured by participants' level of agreement or disagreement with the statement, "When I think of [Democrats/Republicans], violent people come to mind" (1-9 scale, "Strongly disagree" to "Strongly agree").
Generalized beliefs about outparty aggressiveness were then measured as in Study 2.
As in Study 2, we used the murder vignette and, to assess misperceptions for nonpolitically-motivated, non-violent crime, the drug trafficking vignette.
Participants' own support and ingroup, outgroup, and meta-perceptions were measured using identical procedures to Study 1.
Perceived support among outgroup and ingroup leaders, as well as the most extreme outgroup and ingroup members, were measured using identical procedures to Study 2.

We also measured ingrouphttps://paperpile.com/c/nmfLz0/WkVXi+6Erub outgroup, and metaperceptions of affect using standard feeling thermometers (42, 43) , and we measured participants' own concern about a potential civil war using identical procedures to Studies 1 and 2.
text.formatted: We also measured ingroup, outgroup, and metaperceptions of affect using standard feeling thermometers <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(42,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">43)</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://paperpile.com/c/nmfLz0/WkVXi+6Erub">,</ref> and we measured participants' own concern about a potential civil war using identical procedures to Studies 1 and 2.

text.text: Finally, we use the same attention check as in Study 2.
We recruited a large sample of Indian participants (N = 2,732) from Cint during 07/30/2026 -08/03/2026.

As described below, we excluded participants in order to obtain a sample of English-speaking Indian participants who supported one of India's two major political alliances: the National Democratic Alliance (N.D.A.), a coalition led by the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), and the Indian National Developmental Inclusive Alliance (I.N.D.I.A.), an opposition coalition primarily led by the Indian National Congress (INC).
We recruited a politically representative sample using quotas based on participants' selfreported party affiliation (BJP, INC, CPI, AAP, BSP, NPP, or another party).

As preregistered (https://researchbox.org/4077&PEER_REVIEW_passcode=VXOCYQ), we excluded participants who did not identify as supporters of either the N.D.A. alliance or the I.N.D.I.A. alliance (697 participants), who failed either of two Englishcomprehension items (1,327 participants), or who failed an attention check (88 participants).
text.formatted: As preregistered (<ref type="url" target="https://researchbox.org/4077&PEER_REVIEW_passcode=VXOCYQ">https://researchbox.org/4077&PEER_REVIEW_passcode=VXOCYQ</ref>), we excluded participants who did not identify as supporters of either the N.D.A. alliance or the I.N.D.I.A. alliance (697 participants), who failed either of two Englishcomprehension items (1,327 participants), or who failed an attention check (88 participants).

text.text: All remaining participants were included in the analyses (N = 620; 319 I.N.D.I.A. alliance supporters, 301 N.D.A. alliance supporters; 195 female; Mage = 30.4, SDage = 11.1).

Participants first reported which political party they support (BJP, INC, CPI, AAP, BSP, NPP, a different party, or none of the above), whether they consider themselves supporters of the N.D.A. alliance, the I.N.D.I.A. alliance, or neither, and their ideology ("In politics people sometimes talk of 'left' and 'right'.
Where would you place yourself on this scale?"
;0 = left,10 = right).
Participants who identified with either alliance were then assigned the other alliance as their outgroup.
Because the survey was administered in English, participants also completed two English-comprehension items (a short reading-comprehension question and a sentence-completion item).
As in Studies 2 and 3, we used the murder vignette and, to assess misperceptions for nonpolitically-motivated, non-violent crime, the drug trafficking vignette.
The murder vignette was adapted to the Indian context as follows:
Murder: "[name] was convicted of murder.

He was arrested by police after stabbing a prominent [outgroup] member to death. [name] targeted the victim because he believed that the [outgroup] is harmful to the nation's future." where [outgroup] was either "N.D.A. alliance" or "I.N.D.I.A. alliance."
The drug trafficking vignette was identical to that used in Study 2.
Participants' own support and ingroup, outgroup, and meta-perceptions were measured using procedures from Study 1, where [outgroup] was either "N.D.A. alliance" or "I.N.D.I.A. alliance."

For example, to measure perceptions of their outgroup/ingroup, participants were instructed, "Please indicate what percentage of people who support the [outgroup/ingroup] you believe will support [name]'s actions.
(Please use a number from 0 to 100, decimals allowed.)."

To measure concern about outgroup/ingroup extremists, participants were asked to "Please take a moment to think about [outgroup] supporters who support or are willing to engage in politically-motivated violence like stabbing a prominent political figure to death."

Participants then rated how much of a threat these supporters pose to Public Safety, Future Election Security, India's Democracy, and India on a 9-point scale, and rated the importance of protecting against them, using the same procedures as Study 2.

Concern about civil war and perceptions of outgroup/ingroup civil war concern were measured using the same procedures as Studies 1 and 2, with reference to the possibility of a civil war occurring in India.

As in Studies 2 and 3, we measured perceived support for political violence among outgroup and ingroup leaders (e.g., elected officials), as well as among the most extreme outgroup and ingroup supporters, using identical procedures to Study 2, and we assessed perceptions of whether typical outgroup members are more aggressive than typical ingroup members ("The typical [outgroup] supporter is more aggressive than the typical [ingroup] supporter"; 1-9 scale).
We also measured ingroup, outgroup, and metaperceptions of affect using standard feeling thermometers (42, 43).
text.formatted: We also measured ingroup, outgroup, and metaperceptions of affect using standard feeling thermometers <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(42,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">43)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, as an attention check, participants were asked, "What was NOT covered in this study?"
with the following randomly-ordered response options: Murder, Selling drugs, Civil war, and Crashing a plane.
Participants who did not select "Crashing a plane" were excluded from all analyses.
